figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of AttnSR. Actor replay supplies attention for a step graph. Backtracking from the terminal step, recency correction, and layer fusion yield an allocation, and confidence and the centered outcome scale it into signed intermediate rewards. The outcome reward is retained. Graph edges link later steps to earlier dependencies, and episode indices are omitted.
figures.headline: Token attention becomes a step graph whose backtracked, layer-fused allocation scales signed intermediate rewards.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 illustrates how token attention becomes a step graph for reward construction.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Integration of AttnSR into actor–critic RL. (a) The PPO integration of AttnSR adds intermediate rewards while retaining the outcome reward. (b) Detached actor attention supplies rewards, and pre-update critic values support GAE and target construction. Normalized advantages guide the actor, while estimated returns supervise the critic as in Equation 14. Targets remain fixed during optimization. Solid arrows carry signals or targets, and dashed arrows denote updates.
figures.headline: Detached actor attention supplies intermediate rewards that change PPO advantages and value targets while the PPO losses stay unchanged.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 shows how detached actor attention changes policy advantages and value targets through intermediate rewards, retaining the PPO losses.

Figure 4 reports greedy evaluation of every checkpoint on all 274 held-out tasks.

abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. AttnSR traces backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response. The terminal step, measured relative to a running baseline, determines whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps. In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, AttnSR consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%. The ablation experiment shows that the benefit depends on how intermediate rewards are assigned, rather than simple accumulation of step rewards over time. AttnSR also improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9%. These results support policy attention as a practical prior for step-level reward allocation in long-horizon agentic RL. Code is available at https://github.com/fairyshine/AttnSR.

sections.body: The paper addresses credit assignment in long-horizon agent RL, where PPO with an outcome reward gives little per-step signal. AttnSR derives intermediate rewards from policy attention collected during training replay, with no separate reward model or extra rollouts. Attention is treated as a relevance prior, not evidence of causal contribution. In the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, ALFWorld success rises from 91.2% to 97.1%, and the positional ablation reaches 92.3%. On ScienceWorld, AttnSR gives higher official scores at all four reported checkpoints and 29.9% fewer mean environment steps.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Outcome-only RL gives little per-step supervision to long-horizon LLM agents, so AttnSR derives step rewards from policy attention.

sections.body: Each episode is a multi-turn conversation of K decision steps, with an outcome reward in [0,1]. For terminal-only PPO, that reward is placed at the final assistant endpoint. Observation tokens are masked from the actor and critic losses. AttnSR keeps the final reward and adds a signed shaping reward at each intermediate step endpoint, so the token reward sequence is the baseline plus these step terms. The goal is to derive the step rewards from actor attention and terminal outcomes. For WebShop and ScienceWorld, binary success is an evaluation threshold, not the training reward. Format-error trajectories receive reward 0.
sections.heading: Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Terminal-only PPO puts the outcome at the final step, and AttnSR adds signed intermediate rewards without changing that final reward.

sections.body: Attention from each assistant message to earlier assistant and observation messages is summed per layer, and the six selected layers each form a step graph. Relevance is traced backward from the final step with decay 0.85 per hop. A recency correction and geometric fusion across layers then give an allocation over intermediate steps. A confidence gate uses covered terminal mass and allocation entropy. The outcome is centered on a running baseline, and the budget scale is 0.25, so intermediate rewards sum in absolute value to at most 0.25. Limits: attention indicates relevance, not contribution; the shaped return is not guaranteed to be policy invariant; wall-clock and peak-memory overheads are unmeasured.
sections.heading: AttnSR: Actor Attention for Step Credit
sections.headline: Attention is traced backward from the final step, gated by confidence, and centered on outcome to set signed step rewards.

sections.body: Experiments use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with rank-64 LoRA, matched against token-level PPO, on ALFWorld (274 held-out tasks), WebShop (500), and ScienceWorld (1,819). At epoch 4, ALFWorld success rises from 91.24% to 97.08% (266/274). An exact McNemar test gives p=0.002 and a 95% gain interval of [+2.55,+9.49] points. ScienceWorld official score goes from 44.53% to 46.35%, with unadjusted p=0.040 that does not survive Bonferroni correction. WebShop success rises from 40.20% to 41.00%, while official score falls from 70.74% to 69.71%. Results come from single runs, and PPO and GRPO optimization budgets differ.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Paired tests show the ALFWorld gain at p=0.002, while the ScienceWorld gain does not survive multiple-comparison correction.

sections.body: Agentic RL work addresses credit assignment through several routes. POAD, ArCHer and GiGPO change how value or advantage is estimated across turns or steps. VinePPO uses Monte Carlo rollouts, AgentPRM learns progress, TARL uses an LLM judge, and SWEET-RL trains an evaluator with privileged information. AttnSR instead intervenes at the reward interface, assigning outcome-conditioned rewards that then enter the target computation of RL algorithms. Unlike the return-preserving redistribution in RUDDER, AttnSR keeps the outcome reward and adds intermediate rewards, so it changes the return without guaranteeing policy invariance.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Other agent credit methods use rollouts, learned evaluators or value estimation changes, whereas AttnSR changes only the reward interface.

sections.body: AttnSR allocates outcome-conditioned rewards from actor attention, without extra rollouts or a learned reward model. Under PPO, ALFWorld success rises from 91.2% to 97.1%, exceeding the linear control. ScienceWorld shows numerical gains with fewer interactions, while WebShop has no statistically detectable gain. Supplementary GRPO token-advantage results come from one training run per method. Future work will extend evaluation to longer context lengths and interaction horizons, and to action dependencies spanning more distant steps.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: AttnSR raises ALFWorld success from 91.2% to 97.1% under PPO, with no detectable WebShop gain and one run per method.

sections.body: Table 4 gives official scores at four checkpoints, including ALFWorld 91.24 for PPO and 97.08 for AttnSR at epoch 4. Table 6 gives ALFWorld task-family success at epoch 4. Appendix C and Tables 8 and 9 list the implementation and hyperparameters, including attention layers 8 to 18 and query blocks of 128 tokens. Appendix D reports paired McNemar p-values and bootstrap intervals for ALFWorld, WebShop and ScienceWorld. Appendix E covers inference-trajectory diagnostics and exact-input matching, and Table 16 gives the notation.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists checkpoint scores, ALFWorld family results, hyperparameters, paired significance, trajectory diagnostics and notation.
